subject: literature
title: Négritude (c. 1928–1960): Black writers in French claim a word and a world
dek: In interwar Paris, students and writers from Martinique, Senegal, French Guiana, Haiti and Madagascar met in salons, lecture halls and little magazines and began to answer the French empire in its own language. Out of that meeting came Négritude: a word Aimé Césaire forged from an insult, a body of poetry by Césaire, Léopold Sédar Senghor and Léon-Gontran Damas, and a debate about Black identity that ran from the Nardal sisters' salon in Clamart to the 1956 Congress of Black Writers and Artists at the Sorbonne, and then on into the politics of decolonisation.

thumb.alt: Front page of the first issue of L'Étudiant noir, March 1935

hero.alt: Portrait of Léopold Sédar Senghor printed in a newspaper in 1958
hero.caption: Léopold Sédar Senghor in a newspaper portrait from September 1958. By then the poet who had arrived in Paris as a student in 1928 was a deputy in the French National Assembly; two years later he became the first president of independent Senegal.
hero.credit: Unknown photographer, Présence Congolaise (1958) / Public domain

honesty: Négritude is usually told as the story of three young men, Césaire, Senghor and Damas, and this capsule follows that outline because their poems are the core of the movement. But the outline leaves people out. Jane and Paulette Nardal were writing about Black consciousness and running a salon for Black intellectuals in Paris several years before the word négritude appeared, and Paulette Nardal complained in 1960 that their role had been forgotten. Suzanne Césaire wrote some of the sharpest essays of the Martinican wartime phase. The movement's founders also disagreed with each other: Senghor's version stressed a distinct African sensibility, while Césaire and Damas were closer to revolt and to Marxism. The dates c. 1928–1960 are a teaching frame, running from Jane Nardal's essay on Black internationalism to the year most of French West Africa became independent. Exact dates for some events, such as the first appearance of the word, differ between sources; where they differ, this capsule follows the published record and says so.

timeline.label: Jane Nardal's “Internationalisme noir”
timeline.detail: In February 1928 the first issue of La Dépêche africaine, a Paris newspaper for Black readers, carries Jane Nardal's essay “Internationalisme noir” (Black internationalism). She argues that Black people in Africa, the Caribbean and the United States are becoming aware of a shared condition. In October she follows it with “Pantins exotiques” (Exotic puppets), about Paris's fascination with Black women as exotic entertainment.

timeline.label: Colonial Exhibition; La Revue du monde noir
timeline.detail: From May to November 1931 the International Colonial Exhibition in the Bois de Vincennes presents the French empire to millions of visitors, with reconstructed temples and villages. The Surrealists publish a tract urging people not to visit. In October Paulette Nardal and the Haitian scholar Léo Sajous launch La Revue du monde noir, a bilingual French and English magazine. It runs for six issues, until April 1932.

timeline.label: Légitime Défense
timeline.detail: A group of Martinican students in Paris, including Étienne Léro, René Ménil and Jules Monnerot, publish a single issue of Légitime Défense (Self-Defence). It combines Surrealism and Marxism and attacks Caribbean poets who imitate French models. The issue causes a scandal and there is no second one.

timeline.label: L'Étudiant noir
timeline.detail: The first issue of L'Étudiant noir, the journal of the Association of Martinican Students in France, appears in March 1935. Césaire, Senghor and Damas all write for it. In the May–June issue Césaire's essay “Conscience raciale et révolution sociale” uses the word négritude, the earliest printed use usually cited. Only two issues survive.

timeline.label: Damas, Pigments
timeline.detail: Léon-Gontran Damas publishes Pigments with the small Paris press of Guy Lévis Mano, with a preface by the Surrealist poet Robert Desnos. It is the first book of Négritude poetry. French authorities later ban it as a threat to state security.

timeline.label: Cahier d'un retour au pays natal
timeline.detail: In August 1939, after a rejection elsewhere, the Paris magazine Volontés publishes Césaire's long poem Cahier d'un retour au pays natal (Notebook of a Return to the Native Land). Césaire is already sailing home to Martinique to teach. The same year Senghor publishes his essay “Ce que l'homme noir apporte” (What the Black Man Contributes).

timeline.label: Tropiques and Breton
timeline.detail: In Martinique, under the Vichy administration, Aimé Césaire, Suzanne Césaire and René Ménil found the review Tropiques. In April André Breton, leaving wartime France on his way to New York, finds the first issue in a Fort-de-France shop and meets Césaire. The review continues, despite censorship, until 1945.

timeline.label: Senghor's anthology and “Orphée noir”
timeline.detail: Senghor publishes the Anthologie de la nouvelle poésie nègre et malgache de langue française. Jean-Paul Sartre's preface, “Orphée noir” (Black Orpheus), introduces Négritude to the wider French intellectual public and calls it an “anti-racist racism”, a stage in a dialectic that would eventually be overcome.

timeline.label: First Congress of Black Writers and Artists
timeline.detail: In September 1956 Alioune Diop and the journal Présence Africaine hold the First International Congress of Black Writers and Artists at the Sorbonne. Speakers and participants include Césaire, Senghor, Frantz Fanon, Richard Wright, Jean Price-Mars, Cheikh Anta Diop and Jacques Rabemananjara. Pablo Picasso designs the poster.

timeline.label: Independence
timeline.detail: Senegal and most of France's sub-Saharan colonies become independent states. On 5 September 1960 Senghor is elected the first president of Senegal. Césaire, by contrast, remains mayor of Fort-de-France and a deputy in Paris, representing an island that became a French department in 1946 at his own urging.

sections.title: An empire that taught its subjects to be French, and a Paris that wanted them exotic

blocks.text: To understand Négritude you have to start with the way France ruled. Britain often governed its colonies through local rulers and spoke of separate peoples developing separately. France spoke the language of assimilation: in principle, a colonial subject who learned French, studied French literature and absorbed French values could become French. In practice, very few people were offered that path, and those who took it were expected to leave the rest of themselves behind. In the old Caribbean colonies of Martinique, Guadeloupe and French Guiana, where slavery had been abolished in 1848, a Black and mixed-race middle class had grown up that took French schooling very seriously. In West Africa, a tiny educated elite was trained in mission and government schools. The brightest students from both places were sent to Paris.

The Paris they found in the 1920s was full of Black culture, but mostly on white terms. Jazz had arrived with American soldiers and musicians after the First World War. Josephine Baker became a star in La Revue nègre in 1925. Collectors and artists such as Picasso had been buying African masks and sculpture for two decades. This fashion for things nègre was not the same thing as respect. It treated Black people as rhythm, instinct and decoration. The word nègre itself, like its English equivalent, was an insult.

blocks.alt: French postage stamp for the 1931 International Colonial Exhibition, Paris, showing figures representing the colonies
blocks.caption: A 1.50-franc French stamp issued for the International Colonial Exhibition in Paris in 1931, designed by Joseph de la Nézière. The exhibition, held in the Bois de Vincennes from May to November, presented the empire as a family of peoples under French protection. The young writers of Négritude were students in Paris that year.
blocks.credit: Joseph de la Nézière, 1931 / Public domain

blocks.text: The International Colonial Exhibition of 1931 showed the official picture at its grandest. In the Bois de Vincennes, visitors could walk from a full-scale copy of the temple of Angkor Wat to model villages from West Africa. The message was that France was bringing civilisation to grateful peoples. The Surrealists published a tract called “Ne visitez pas l'Exposition coloniale” (Do not visit the Colonial Exhibition), and the Communist Party organised a small counter-exhibition on the truth about the colonies. For the Black students in Paris, the exhibition was a daily reminder of how they were seen.

Two other currents reached them from across the Atlantic. The first was the Harlem Renaissance. Students in Paris read Claude McKay, whose novel Banjo (1929) is set among Black dockworkers and drifters in Marseille, and Langston Hughes, whose poems were translated in Paris magazines. Alain Locke's anthology The New Negro (1925) offered the idea that Black people could define their own culture rather than wait to be described. The second current came from Haiti, the first Black republic. In Ainsi parla l'oncle (So Spoke the Uncle, 1928), the Haitian ethnologist Jean Price-Mars told Haiti's educated class to stop being ashamed of the peasant culture, the Creole language and the Vodou religion that they had inherited from Africa. Césaire later called Haiti the place where négritude stood up for the first time.

Many accounts of Négritude begin in 1935. A better starting point is a few years earlier, with two Martinican sisters. Jane and Paulette Nardal came from a well-off Black family in Martinique and studied in Paris in the 1920s. In February 1928 Jane Nardal published “Internationalisme noir” in the first issue of La Dépêche africaine, a newspaper for Black readers. She argued that Black people across the world were waking up to a shared history and could form a kind of international community without giving up the cultures they had acquired. Later that year her essay “Pantins exotiques” (Exotic puppets) took apart the Parisian craze for Black women as entertainers. These are, in substance, the arguments that the better-known men would make later.

sections.title: From the Clamart salon to L'Étudiant noir, the Cahier and the anthology

blocks.text: At the end of the 1920s the Nardal sisters began hosting a salon at the family's home in Clamart, just outside Paris. Students and writers from the Caribbean and Africa met African Americans passing through Paris, and they talked, in French and English, about race, colonialism, jazz and literature. Senghor later wrote that he and his friends were in contact with Black Americans between 1929 and 1934 through Paulette Nardal's salon. Paulette Nardal had been one of the first Black students at the Sorbonne, where she studied English, and she translated Harlem writers for French readers.

blocks.caption: Paulette Nardal (1896–1985), photographed in the 1920s. With her sister Jane she ran the Clamart salon, and in 1931 she co-founded La Revue du monde noir. She later worked as a journalist, served at the United Nations, and founded a women's organisation in Martinique.

blocks.text: In October 1931 Paulette Nardal and the Haitian doctor and scholar Léo Sajous launched La Revue du monde noir (The Review of the Black World). It was printed in both French and English and published poems, essays on African history and art, and news of Black life in the United States and the Caribbean. It was deliberately polite and avoided open politics, partly because it received some money from the Ministry of the Colonies. It lasted six issues. In the last one, Paulette Nardal's essay “Éveil de la conscience de race” (The Awakening of Race Consciousness) described how Caribbean students in Paris had moved from wanting to be indistinguishable from the French to taking an interest in Africa.

Some Martinican students wanted something angrier. In June 1932 Étienne Léro, René Ménil, Jules Monnerot and a few friends published Légitime Défense (Self-Defence), a single issue that mixed Surrealism with Marxism. It mocked Caribbean poets who wrote polite French verse about palm trees and pretty Creole women, and it accused the Caribbean middle class of imitating its oppressors. The issue caused a scandal among the students' families, and it never had a sequel, but it introduced a combination that would matter later: a poetics of revolt borrowed from Surrealism, joined to an anti-colonial politics.

The three men usually named as the founders of Négritude met in this world. Aimé Césaire, born in 1913 in Basse-Pointe on the north coast of Martinique, came to Paris in 1931 on a scholarship to the Lycée Louis-le-Grand, the elite school that prepared students for the École normale supérieure. On his first day there, Césaire later recalled, he met Léopold Sédar Senghor, seven years older, born in 1906 in the coastal town of Joal in Senegal, who had come to Paris to study in 1928. Léon-Gontran Damas, born in 1912 in Cayenne in French Guiana, had been at school with Césaire in Martinique and was studying law and ethnology in Paris. Senghor introduced Césaire to Africa as a living culture rather than a schoolbook abstraction; Césaire gave Senghor his combative energy.

blocks.alt: Front page of L'Étudiant noir, issue 1, March 1935
blocks.caption: The first issue of L'Étudiant noir, dated March 1935, the newspaper of the Association of Martinican Students in France. Its first page is mostly about student matters, such as scholarships. In the May–June issue, Césaire's article on racial consciousness and social revolution used the word négritude.
blocks.credit: Association des étudiants martiniquais en France, 1935 / CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)

blocks.text: In 1935 the friends turned the newsletter of the Martinican students' association into L'Étudiant noir (The Black Student). Damas later described the aim: they had stopped being Martinican, Guadeloupean, Guianese, African or Malagasy students and had become one and the same Black student. In the May–June 1935 issue, Césaire published “Conscience raciale et révolution sociale” (Racial Consciousness and Social Revolution), under a rubric called “Nègreries”. He rejected assimilation, the idea that the way forward was to become as French as possible, and he used the word nègre as a term of pride. This is the earliest printed use of négritude usually cited. The word took the insult and added the suffix -itude, as in solitude or servitude, to name a condition. Senghor later said that the word had been contested as a word before it was contested as a concept.

The first book of Négritude poetry was by Damas. Pigments, published in 1937 by the small press of Guy Lévis Mano with a preface by the Surrealist poet Robert Desnos, is short, rhythmic and sarcastic. Its best-known poems are about the costume of assimilation. In “Solde” (Sale), dedicated to Césaire, the speaker repeats that he feels ridiculous in their shoes, their dinner jacket, their shirt-front, their stiff collar, their monocle and their bowler hat. In “Hoquet” (Hiccup), a mother's voice keeps correcting a boy's manners and telling him not to behave like a nègre, and the hiccup becomes the memory he cannot swallow. French authorities later banned the book as a threat to state security.

Césaire's Cahier d'un retour au pays natal (Notebook of a Return to the Native Land) is the movement's masterpiece. He began it in the mid-1930s while staying with his friend Petar Guberina on the Dalmatian coast of Yugoslavia. After one magazine turned it down, the Paris review Volontés printed it in August 1939, just as Césaire was returning home to teach. The poem moves from disgust to acceptance. It opens on a Martinique of hunger, sickness and apathy, describes the speaker's shame at laughing along with others at a poor Black man on a tram, and ends with a man standing up. In its most quoted passage the speaker defines his blackness by what it is not: “my négritude is not a stone, its deafness hurled against the clamour of the day / my négritude is not a speck of dead water on the dead eye of the earth / my négritude is neither a tower nor a cathedral / it plunges into the red flesh of the soil / it plunges into the burning flesh of the sky.” The poem got almost no attention in 1939. Its fame came after the war.

The Second World War split the group. Senghor, by then a teacher with a French agrégation in grammar, was drafted into a colonial infantry regiment and captured by the Germans in June 1940. He spent two years in prisoner-of-war camps, where he wrote many of the poems later published as Hosties noires (Black Hosts, 1948), until he was released on medical grounds in 1942. Césaire and his wife, Suzanne Césaire, were teaching at the Lycée Schoelcher in Fort-de-France, where one of their pupils was a teenager named Frantz Fanon. Martinique was governed by Admiral Georges Robert in the name of the Vichy regime, with a large garrison of sailors on the island and strict censorship.

In April 1941 the Césaires, René Ménil and a few colleagues began Tropiques, a review that presented itself as a cultural magazine about Martinican folklore, plants and poetry, which was the only way to get past the censors. Under that cover it published essays against colonial culture and Surrealist poems. The same month, André Breton arrived in Martinique on a ship of refugees bound for the Americas, along with the painter Wifredo Lam and the anthropologist Claude Lévi-Strauss. Breton came across the first issue of Tropiques in a shop, met Césaire, and became his champion. His essay “Un grand poète noir” (A Great Black Poet) became the preface to the 1947 editions of the Cahier, which made Césaire famous in Paris and New York.

After the war, Négritude became a public movement. In 1945 Césaire was elected mayor of Fort-de-France and a deputy in the French National Assembly, with Communist support, and Senghor was elected deputy for Senegal. In 1947 the Senegalese philosopher Alioune Diop founded the journal Présence Africaine in Paris, which became the movement's main platform and, from 1949, a publishing house. In 1948, for the centenary of the abolition of slavery, Senghor published his Anthologie de la nouvelle poésie nègre et malgache de langue française (Anthology of the New Black and Malagasy Poetry in French). Its preface, by Jean-Paul Sartre, was called “Orphée noir” (Black Orpheus). Sartre praised the poets as the most revolutionary poetry of the time, but he also described Négritude as an “anti-racist racism” and as the weak stage in a dialectic that would be overcome by a universal, class-based revolution. The preface made Négritude famous among French intellectuals and gave its critics their first line of attack.

sections.title: Three founders, three different ideas of blackness

blocks.text: Négritude showed up mostly as poetry, essays and magazines, and later as speeches, conferences and government cultural policy. The three founders shared a starting point, the refusal to be ashamed of being Black, but they took it in different directions.

people.name: Aimé Césaire
people.text: Poet, playwright and politician from Martinique. His Cahier d'un retour au pays natal (1939) is the movement's central poem, and his Discours sur le colonialisme (Discourse on Colonialism, 1950, revised 1955) is one of the most influential anti-colonial essays ever written. It argues that colonisation degrades the coloniser and that Nazism was colonial violence turned back on Europe. For Césaire, négritude was the fact of being Black, the acceptance of that fact, and the taking up of a history that included the slave trade and the plantation. His later plays include La Tragédie du roi Christophe (1963), about a king of post-revolutionary Haiti, and Une Tempête (1969), a rewriting of Shakespeare's The Tempest from Caliban's side. He was mayor of Fort-de-France from 1945 to 2001 and left the Communist Party in 1956.

people.name: Léopold Sédar Senghor
people.text: Poet and statesman from Senegal. His collections Chants d'ombre (Shadow Songs, 1945) and Hosties noires (Black Hosts, 1948) use long, chanting lines modelled partly on the praise poetry of his Serer childhood, and are meant to be read aloud with drums or the kora. His version of Négritude stressed a distinct African way of knowing, which he summed up in a 1939 sentence his critics never let him forget: “L'émotion est nègre, comme la raison hellène” (Emotion is Black, as reason is Greek). He was the first president of Senegal from 1960 to 1980, governed for long periods as the head of a one-party state, and was the first African elected to the Académie française, in 1983.

people.name: Léon-Gontran Damas
people.text: Poet from French Guiana, of mixed African, European and Indigenous American descent. His Pigments (1937) was the first book of Négritude poetry, and it remains the most direct: short lines, repetition, jazz rhythm and open sarcasm about the manners he had been taught. He was elected a deputy for French Guiana from 1948 to 1951, edited the anthology Poètes d'expression française, and spent his last years teaching at Howard University in Washington, D.C., where he died in 1978. He is the least famous of the three today, and many readers find him the most modern.

blocks.alt: Aimé Césaire in old age, wearing glasses, photographed in 2003
blocks.caption: Aimé Césaire in November 2003, aged ninety. He had been mayor of the city for almost six decades and stepped down in 2001. When he died in 2008 he was given a state funeral, and a plaque in his honour was placed in the Panthéon in Paris in 2011.

blocks.text: Senghor's most famous poem, “Femme noire” (Black Woman), from Chants d'ombre, begins “Femme nue, femme noire / Vêtue de ta couleur qui est vie, de ta forme qui est beauté” (Naked woman, black woman, / clothed in your colour which is life, in your form which is beauty). It was a deliberate reversal of a culture that treated Black women's bodies as either ugly or comic. It is also a good example of why later readers, including feminist critics, have questioned the movement: the woman in the poem does not speak. She is a landscape and a symbol of Africa, admired by a male poet.

blocks.alt: Léon-Gontran Damas seated, in a suit, at a conference in 1972
blocks.caption: Léon-Gontran Damas at the Second Congress of African People in San Diego in 1972. By then he had moved to Washington, D.C., where he taught at Georgetown and then Howard University until his death in 1978.

blocks.text: Two women deserve a place in this section, not a footnote. Paulette Nardal's salon and magazine created the network in which the founders met Harlem writers, and her essays described the awakening of race consciousness before the word négritude existed. Suzanne Césaire, born Suzanne Roussi in 1915, published seven essays in Tropiques between 1941 and 1945. In “Le grand camouflage” (The Great Camouflage, 1945), she described how the beauty of the Caribbean landscape hid hunger and racial humiliation from the people who admired it. In “1943: Le surréalisme et nous” she argued that Surrealism could help Martinicans break out of the opposition between Black and white, African and European, savage and civilised. She stopped publishing after 1945, and her essays were only collected in English in 2012.

Around these figures was a much larger group of writers whom Senghor's 1948 anthology helped make visible. They included the Senegalese storyteller and poet Birago Diop, whose Les Contes d'Amadou Koumba (1947) retold Wolof folktales he had heard from a griot; the poet David Diop, whose Coups de pilon (Pounding, 1956) is angrier than Senghor's work; the Malagasy poets Jean-Joseph Rabearivelo and Jacques Rabemananjara; the Guadeloupean poet Guy Tirolien; and Haitian writers such as Jacques Roumain, whose novel Gouverneurs de la rosée (Masters of the Dew, 1944) is about peasants trying to bring water back to a drought-stricken village.

The movement's high point as a gathering was the First International Congress of Black Writers and Artists, organised by Présence Africaine at the Sorbonne in September 1956. Delegates from Africa, the Caribbean and the United States met in the Amphithéâtre Descartes while, outside, the Algerian war was escalating. Césaire spoke on culture and colonisation; Fanon, by then a psychiatrist working in Algeria, spoke on racism and culture. The American novelist Richard Wright attended, and James Baldwin reported on the congress in his essay “Princes and Powers”, where he noticed how hard it was to find a common Black culture shared by a Senegalese poet, a Martinican deputy and an American from Harlem. That question, whether one blackness exists across such different histories, was the movement's deepest problem.

sections.title: Harlem, Havana, Port-au-Prince, Lisbon and Manchester

blocks.text: Négritude was one of several movements in the 1920s to 1950s in which Black writers rejected the image of themselves they had been given. They knew about each other, but each grew out of its own colonial or national situation.

items: In the United States, the Harlem Renaissance of the 1920s came first and influenced the Paris students directly through Claude McKay, Langston Hughes and Alain Locke. The difference is that Harlem writers were demanding full citizenship in the country where they were born, while the Négritude writers were colonial subjects who were also arguing about the relationship between their islands or territories and France.

In Cuba, the poets of negrismo or poesía negra in the late 1920s and 1930s brought Afro-Cuban rhythms and speech into poetry. Nicolás Guillén's Motivos de son (1930) wrote poems in the form of the son, a popular Afro-Cuban song style. Some of this movement was written by white poets fascinated by Black culture, which is a difference from Négritude.

In Haiti, after the United States occupation began in 1915, indigénisme turned writers toward peasant culture, Creole and Vodou. Jean Price-Mars's Ainsi parla l'oncle (1928) was its founding book, and Jacques Roumain's novels carried it into fiction. Haitian writers appeared in Senghor's anthology, and Price-Mars attended the 1956 congress.

In Portuguese Africa, students from Angola, Mozambique and Cape Verde in Lisbon in the late 1940s and 1950s, including the Angolan poet Agostinho Neto and the critic Mário Pinto de Andrade, read Négritude poetry and began writing poems about African identity. Several later led liberation movements, and Neto became the first president of Angola in 1975.

In the British empire, the Fifth Pan-African Congress in Manchester in October 1945 brought together Kwame Nkrumah, Jomo Kenyatta and W. E. B. Du Bois and called for independence. Anglophone Pan-Africanism was more openly political and less literary than Négritude, and many Anglophone writers later rejected Négritude's emphasis on race.

blocks.text: The comparison shows what was particular about Négritude. Because France claimed that its subjects could become French through language and education, the revolt against assimilation took the form of a revolt inside the French language. Césaire and Senghor wrote some of the most ambitious French poetry of the century while arguing that French civilisation was not the measure of all civilisations.

sections.title: Critics, independence, and the generations that answered back

blocks.text: The sharpest early critic was Césaire's own former pupil. In Peau noire, masques blancs (Black Skin, White Masks, 1952), Frantz Fanon described the experience of being seen as Black on a Paris street and wrote that he had found comfort in Négritude, only to have Sartre's “Orphée noir” tell him that his blackness was a passing stage in someone else's dialectic. In Les Damnés de la terre (The Wretched of the Earth, 1961) he went further. In the chapter on national culture he argued that a generalised African or Black culture was a reaction to colonial racism, which had lumped all Africans together, and that real national cultures would be made in the struggle for liberation, not by recovering a lost past.

Writers from English-speaking Africa were often impatient with the whole idea. The Nigerian playwright Wole Soyinka is remembered for a line usually quoted as “A tiger does not proclaim its tigritude; it pounces.” His point was that confident writing does not need to announce its identity. Others criticised Senghor's claim about emotion and reason as a mirror image of colonial racism, which had also said that Africans were emotional rather than rational.

Politically, the founders went different ways. Senghor became president of Senegal in 1960 and made Négritude something close to a state ideology. In April 1966 Dakar hosted the World Festival of Negro Arts, with performers and writers from Africa, the Caribbean and the United States, including Duke Ellington. Critics at home pointed out that Senghor's government also kept close ties with France and suppressed political opponents. Césaire, who had pushed through the 1946 law that made Martinique a French department, broke with the French Communist Party in October 1956 with his Lettre à Maurice Thorez, after the Soviet crushing of the Hungarian uprising, and founded his own Martinican Progressive Party in 1958. He never campaigned for Martinican independence.

In the Caribbean, later writers answered Négritude by moving away from Africa as the main point of reference. Édouard Glissant, also from Martinique, proposed Antillanité, an identity based on the mixed, multilingual history of the Caribbean itself, set out most fully in Le Discours antillais (Caribbean Discourse, 1981). In 1989 Jean Bernabé, Patrick Chamoiseau and Raphaël Confiant published Éloge de la créolité (In Praise of Creoleness), which begins by calling themselves neither Europeans, nor Africans, nor Asians, but Creoles, and which acknowledges Césaire as a forerunner while rejecting his focus on Africa. Chamoiseau's novel Texaco won the Prix Goncourt in 1992.

Since the 1990s Négritude has been read again more sympathetically. Scholars such as T. Denean Sharpley-Whiting have restored the Nardal sisters and Suzanne Césaire to the story, and the Senegalese philosopher Souleymane Bachir Diagne has read Senghor as a serious philosopher of art rather than a naive believer in racial essences. Césaire's Discourse on Colonialism is now taught across the world as a founding text of postcolonial thought. In the United States, the poets of the Black Arts Movement of the 1960s, who had their own slogan “Black is beautiful”, saw Négritude as an earlier version of their own project.

Négritude began by taking an insult and turning it into a name to be proud of. Its critics said that this kept the movement tied to the very racial categories it was fighting. When a group reclaims a word or an identity that was used against it, does it escape the old categories, or does it confirm them? Try answering for Césaire's Cahier, for Senghor's “Femme noire”, and for one example from your own time.

read.note: A general article with the word's history, the movement's influences, and its later critics.

fun_fact.title: André Breton found Césaire's magazine while buying a ribbon
fun_fact.text: In April 1941 André Breton, the leader of the Surrealists, was stuck in Martinique on his way from wartime France to New York, watched by the Vichy police. Walking around Fort-de-France, he went into a haberdashery to buy a ribbon for his daughter and saw, among the sewing goods, the first issue of a new magazine called Tropiques. The magazine was paid for and distributed by its own founders, and this shop was kept by the sister of René Ménil, one of them. The town's bookshops, meanwhile, had almost nothing on their shelves. Through her Breton met Ménil and then Aimé Césaire. Breton later called Césaire's Cahier “nothing less than the greatest lyrical monument of our times”, and his essay about that meeting became the preface that made the poem famous.

glossary.explain: A literary and intellectual movement of French-speaking Black writers from Africa and the Caribbean, from the late 1920s to about 1960. It rejected the French policy of cultural assimilation and asserted the value of Black history and culture. The word was formed by Aimé Césaire in the 1930s from the insult nègre plus the suffix -itude.
The French colonial idea that colonial subjects could and should become culturally French through language and education. Négritude writers saw it as a demand to give up their own history.
French word for a Black person that was used as an insult, like its English equivalent. Négritude writers deliberately took it up as a term of pride.

Martinican poet, playwright and politician (1913–2008). Author of Cahier d'un retour au pays natal (1939) and Discours sur le colonialisme (1950). Mayor of Fort-de-France from 1945 to 2001 and a deputy in the French National Assembly for decades.

Senegalese poet and statesman (1906–2001). Author of Chants d'ombre (1945) and Hosties noires (1948), editor of the 1948 anthology of new Black and Malagasy poetry, first president of Senegal (1960–1980), and the first African member of the Académie française (elected 1983).

Poet and politician from French Guiana (1912–1978). His Pigments (1937) was the first book of Négritude poetry. He was a deputy for French Guiana from 1948 to 1951 and later taught at Howard University.

Martinican writer, journalist and translator (1896–1985). With her sister Jane she ran the Clamart salon, and in 1931 she co-founded La Revue du monde noir. Her essays on race consciousness came before the word négritude.
Martinican writer (1900–1993), sister of Paulette Nardal. Her 1928 essay “Internationalisme noir” in La Dépêche africaine argued for a shared consciousness among Black people across the world.
Jane and Paulette Nardal, and their sister Andrée, who hosted the Clamart salon for Black intellectuals near Paris around 1929 to 1934.
The salon held by the Nardal sisters at their home in Clamart, near Paris, where Caribbean, African and African American writers met in the late 1920s and early 1930s.
Jane Nardal's 1928 essay, published in the first issue of La Dépêche africaine, on the awakening of a shared consciousness among Black people in Africa and the diaspora.
Jane Nardal's October 1928 essay criticising the Parisian fashion for Black women as exotic entertainers.
A Paris newspaper for Black readers founded in February 1928. Jane and Paulette Nardal wrote for it.

aliases: The Review of the Black World
glossary.explain: A bilingual French and English magazine founded in October 1931 by Paulette Nardal and Léo Sajous. It published six issues before closing in April 1932.

glossary.term: Éveil de la conscience de race
glossary.explain: Paulette Nardal's essay in the last issue of La Revue du monde noir (1932), describing how Caribbean students in Paris began to take an interest in Africa and in their own race.
Haitian doctor and scholar who co-founded La Revue du monde noir with Paulette Nardal in 1931.

A single-issue magazine published in Paris in June 1932 by Martinican students including Étienne Léro, René Ménil and Jules Monnerot. It combined Surrealism and Marxism and attacked imitative Caribbean poetry.
Martinican poet (1910–1939), one of the authors of Légitime Défense (1932).
Martinican philosopher and writer (1907–2004), co-author of Légitime Défense (1932) and co-founder of Tropiques (1941) with Aimé and Suzanne Césaire.
Martinican-born writer and sociologist (1909–1995), one of the authors of Légitime Défense (1932).

The journal of the Association of Martinican Students in France, first issued in March 1935. Césaire, Senghor and Damas wrote for it, and Césaire's article in the May–June 1935 issue contains the earliest printed use of the word négritude usually cited.
Aimé Césaire's article in L'Étudiant noir (May–June 1935), which rejected assimilation and used the word négritude.
Léon-Gontran Damas's first poetry collection (1937), published by Guy Lévis Mano with a preface by Robert Desnos. The first book of Négritude poetry; later banned by French authorities.
A poem in Damas's Pigments (1937), dedicated to Aimé Césaire, in which the speaker feels ridiculous in the clothes and manners of assimilation.
A poem in Damas's Pigments (1937) in which a mother's voice corrects a boy's manners, and his memory of it returns like a hiccup.
French Surrealist poet (1900–1945) who wrote the preface to Damas's Pigments. He died after deportation to Nazi concentration camps.
French poet, typographer and publisher (1904–1980) whose small press, GLM, published Damas's Pigments in 1937.

glossary.term: Cahier d'un retour au pays natal
aliases: Notebook of a Return to the Native Land
glossary.explain: Aimé Césaire's book-length poem, first published in the Paris magazine Volontés in August 1939 and republished in expanded editions in 1947 and 1956. The central poem of Négritude.
Paris literary magazine that first published Césaire's Cahier d'un retour au pays natal in August 1939.
Aimé Césaire's essay of 1950, revised in 1955, arguing that colonisation degrades the coloniser and comparing Nazism to colonial violence turned back on Europe.
Aimé Césaire's 1963 play about Henri Christophe, a king of northern Haiti after the Haitian Revolution.
Aimé Césaire's 1969 adaptation of Shakespeare's The Tempest, told from the side of the enslaved Caliban.
Aimé Césaire's October 1956 letter announcing that he was leaving the French Communist Party, led by Maurice Thorez.
Martinican writer and teacher (1915–1966). Co-founder of Tropiques, where she published seven essays between 1941 and 1945, including “Le grand camouflage”.
Suzanne Césaire's 1945 essay in Tropiques about how the beauty of the Caribbean landscape hides hunger and racial humiliation.
A review founded in Fort-de-France in April 1941 by Aimé Césaire, Suzanne Césaire and René Ménil. It presented itself as a cultural magazine to get past Vichy censorship and ran until 1945.
French poet (1896–1966), founder and leader of Surrealism. He met Césaire in Martinique in 1941 and wrote the essay “Un grand poète noir” that prefaced the 1947 editions of the Cahier.
André Breton's essay on Césaire, first published in 1943 and used as the preface to the 1947 editions of the Cahier.

Avant-garde literary and artistic movement founded in Paris in the 1920s by André Breton, interested in dreams, the unconscious and revolt against bourgeois order. Several Négritude writers used its techniques.
Cuban painter (1902–1982) of African, Chinese and European descent who sailed to Martinique with Breton in 1941 and became a friend of Césaire.
French anthropologist (1908–2009) who sailed to Martinique on the same refugee ship as Breton in 1941, an episode he describes in Tristes Tropiques.
Léopold Sédar Senghor's first poetry collection (1945). It includes “Femme noire”.
Léopold Sédar Senghor's 1948 poetry collection, including poems written as a prisoner of war and poems about African soldiers in the French army.
A poem by Senghor in Chants d'ombre (1945) that praises a Black woman as beauty and as a symbol of Africa.
Senghor's 1939 essay on the contribution of African culture to humanity. It contains his much-criticised sentence that emotion is Black as reason is Greek.

glossary.term: Anthologie de la nouvelle poésie nègre et malgache de langue française
aliases: Anthologie de la nouvelle poésie nègre et malgache
glossary.explain: Senghor's 1948 anthology of new Black and Malagasy poetry in French, published for the centenary of the abolition of slavery, with a preface by Jean-Paul Sartre.
Jean-Paul Sartre's preface to Senghor's 1948 anthology. It praised the poets but called Négritude an “anti-racist racism” and a stage to be overcome.
Sartre's description of Négritude in “Orphée noir” (1948): a racial self-assertion that answers racism and that, in his view, would eventually give way to a universal class struggle.
French philosopher and writer (1905–1980), leading figure of existentialism. His preface “Orphée noir” (1948) made Négritude famous among French intellectuals.
Journal founded in Paris in November 1947 by Alioune Diop, and from 1949 also a publishing house and bookshop. The main platform of Négritude and of African and Caribbean writing in French.
Senegalese philosopher and editor (1910–1980) who founded Présence Africaine and organised the 1956 Congress of Black Writers and Artists.

glossary.term: First International Congress of Black Writers and Artists
aliases: Congress of Black Writers and Artists
glossary.explain: Gathering organised by Présence Africaine at the Sorbonne in Paris in September 1956, with participants from Africa, the Caribbean and the United States.

Martinican psychiatrist and writer (1925–1961), a former pupil of Aimé Césaire. Author of Peau noire, masques blancs (1952) and Les Damnés de la terre (1961), both of which criticised aspects of Négritude.
Frantz Fanon's 1952 book on the psychology of racism and colonialism, which responds critically to Sartre's “Orphée noir”.
Frantz Fanon's 1961 book on decolonisation. Its chapter on national culture criticises the idea of a single Black or African culture.
African American novelist (1908–1960), author of Native Son, who lived in Paris from 1946 and attended the 1956 congress.
African American writer (1924–1987) who reported on the 1956 congress in his essay “Princes and Powers”.
James Baldwin's essay on the 1956 Congress of Black Writers and Artists, later collected in Nobody Knows My Name (1961).
Senegalese historian and physicist (1923–1986) who argued for the African roots of ancient Egyptian civilisation and attended the 1956 congress.
Malagasy poet and politician (1913–2005), included in Senghor's 1948 anthology and a participant in the 1956 congress.
Malagasy poet (1901 or 1903–1937), one of the first modern African poets in French, included in Senghor's 1948 anthology.
Senegalese poet and storyteller (1906–1989), author of Les Contes d'Amadou Koumba (1947), retellings of Wolof folktales.
Birago Diop's 1947 collection of Wolof folktales, presented as stories told by the griot Amadou Koumba.
Poet of Senegalese and Cameroonian parentage (1927–1960), author of the angry anti-colonial collection Coups de pilon (1956).
David Diop's 1956 poetry collection, one of the most militant books of Négritude poetry.
Guadeloupean poet (1917–1988), a friend of Senghor from the prisoner-of-war camps, included in the 1948 anthology.
Haitian writer and politician (1907–1944), author of the novel Gouverneurs de la rosée (1944) and founder of the Haitian Communist Party.
Jacques Roumain's 1944 novel about Haitian peasants trying to bring water back to their village.
Haitian ethnologist, doctor and diplomat (1876–1969), author of Ainsi parla l'oncle (1928) and founder of Haitian indigénisme.
Jean Price-Mars's 1928 book urging educated Haitians to value their peasant culture, Creole language and Vodou religion.
Haitian literary and cultural movement of the 1920s and 1930s that turned toward peasant culture, Creole and Vodou.
African American cultural movement of the 1920s and early 1930s centred in Harlem, New York. Its writers influenced the Négritude students in Paris.
Jamaican-born writer (1889–1948) of the Harlem Renaissance. His novel Banjo (1929), set among Black workers in Marseille, was widely read by the Paris students.
Claude McKay's 1929 novel about Black dockworkers and drifters in Marseille, important to the young Négritude writers.
African American poet (1901–1967) of the Harlem Renaissance whose poems were translated in Paris magazines and admired by Senghor.
African American philosopher (1885–1954) who edited The New Negro (1925).
Alain Locke's 1925 anthology of the Harlem Renaissance.
American-born dancer and singer (1906–1975) who became a star in Paris in La Revue nègre in 1925.
A large exhibition of the French and other colonial empires held in the Bois de Vincennes, Paris, from May to November 1931.

aliases: Do not visit the Colonial Exhibition
glossary.explain: Surrealist tract of 1931 urging people to boycott the International Colonial Exhibition.
Elite Paris secondary school where Césaire and Senghor met while preparing for the École normale supérieure.
Secondary school in Fort-de-France, Martinique, where Damas and Césaire were pupils and where the Césaires later taught Frantz Fanon.
The French government that collaborated with Nazi Germany from 1940 to 1944. Martinique was ruled in its name by Admiral Georges Robert until 1943.
French admiral (1875–1965) who governed the French Caribbean territories for the Vichy regime from 1940 to 1943.
The 1946 change, sponsored by Césaire, that made Martinique, Guadeloupe, French Guiana and Réunion departments of France rather than colonies.
Martinican writer and philosopher (1928–2011) who proposed Antillanité and later the idea of Relation, moving away from Négritude's focus on Africa.
Édouard Glissant's idea of an identity rooted in the mixed, multilingual history of the Caribbean itself.
Édouard Glissant's 1981 book of essays on Caribbean history and identity.
A 1989 manifesto by Jean Bernabé, Patrick Chamoiseau and Raphaël Confiant that defined Caribbean identity as Creole rather than African or European.
The Caribbean literary movement launched by Éloge de la créolité (1989), which answered Négritude by stressing mixture over African origins.
Martinican novelist (born 1953), co-author of Éloge de la créolité and author of Texaco, which won the Prix Goncourt in 1992.
Martinican linguist (1942–2017), co-author of Éloge de la créolité.
Martinican novelist (born 1951), co-author of Éloge de la créolité.
Patrick Chamoiseau's 1992 novel about a shantytown in Fort-de-France, winner of the Prix Goncourt.
Nigerian playwright and poet (born 1934), winner of the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1986, known for mocking Négritude with a line about a tiger and its tigritude.
Wole Soyinka's mocking coinage, from a line usually quoted as “A tiger does not proclaim its tigritude; it pounces.”
Arts festival held in Dakar, Senegal, in April 1966 under Senghor's sponsorship, with performers and writers from Africa and the diaspora.
American jazz composer and bandleader (1899–1974) who performed at the 1966 World Festival of Negro Arts in Dakar.
Cuban and wider Spanish Caribbean poetic movement of the late 1920s and 1930s that brought Afro-Caribbean rhythms and speech into poetry.
Cuban poet (1902–1989), leading voice of Afro-Cuban poetry, author of Motivos de son (1930).
Nicolás Guillén's 1930 collection of poems written in the form of the Afro-Cuban son.
Angolan poet and doctor (1922–1979), leader of the MPLA liberation movement and the first president of Angola from 1975.
Angolan poet and critic (1928–1990) who studied in Lisbon and Paris, edited anthologies of African poetry in Portuguese, and helped found the MPLA.
Meeting held in Manchester in October 1945 with Kwame Nkrumah, Jomo Kenyatta and W. E. B. Du Bois, which demanded independence for African colonies.
Political and cultural movement for the unity and liberation of Africans and people of African descent.
Ghanaian leader (1909–1972) who led the Gold Coast to independence as Ghana in 1957.
Kenyan leader (c. 1897–1978), first president of Kenya.
African American sociologist, historian and activist (1868–1963), a central figure of Pan-Africanism.
African American artistic movement of the 1960s and 1970s connected to Black Power.
American scholar whose book Negritude Women (2002) restored the Nardal sisters and Suzanne Césaire to the history of the movement.
Senegalese philosopher (born 1955) who has written on Senghor and Négritude as philosophy.
The French academy of language and letters, founded in 1635. Senghor was elected its first African member in 1983.
France's highly competitive examination for senior teachers. Senghor passed it in French grammar in 1935.
Elite Paris institution for training scholars and teachers. Césaire passed its entrance exam in 1935.
The capital of Martinique. Césaire was its mayor from 1945 to 2001.
In West Africa, a hereditary oral historian, storyteller, praise singer and musician.
A West African harp-lute with twenty-one strings, which Senghor imagined as an accompaniment to his poems.
